content.text: Kinetic theory explains gas behaviour by treating a gas as rapidly moving atoms or molecules. Intermolecular forces are often negligible except during collisions. The theory gives molecular interpretations of pressure and temperature and connects macroscopic properties with molecular motion.

Matter is made of atoms and molecules in continual motion. Molecular-scale estimates can be made using density, molar mass and Avogadro’s number. The chapter compares molecular size and spacing to show that molecules occupy a very small fraction of the volume of a gas.
For a sample with mass M and molar mass M₀, the amount in moles is μ = M/M₀ and the number of molecules is N = μNₐ. Avogadro’s number is approximately 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

An ideal gas obeys the equation relating pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas. Temperature must be expressed on the kelvin scale. Real gases approximate ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.
At the same pressure and temperature, equal volumes of ideal gases contain equal numbers of molecules. This follows from the ideal gas equation and is consistent with Avogadro’s hypothesis.

An ideal gas is a theoretical model that obeys the ideal gas equation at all pressures and temperatures. No real gas is perfectly ideal. Real gases approach ideal behaviour when molecules are far apart and intermolecular effects become small, typically at low pressure and high temperature.

metadata.topic: Ideal gas model and real gases

content.text: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. A plot of pressure against volume is approximately hyperbolic under conditions where the gas behaves ideally.
equations: PV = constant at fixed μ and T

content.text: For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is proportional to absolute temperature. The relationship uses kelvin temperature, not Celsius temperature.
equations: V ∝ T at fixed P and μ

content.text: For a mixture of ideal gases in a common vessel at temperature T, the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures each gas would exert alone in the same volume and at the same temperature.
The ideal gas equation can be written in terms of gas density ρ and molar mass M₀. This form is useful when pressure, temperature and density are known.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Density form of ideal gas equation

content.text: A gas consists of a very large number of molecules in random motion. Molecules are small compared with the volume occupied by the gas; interactions are negligible except during collisions; and collisions with each other and container walls are elastic. Newtonian mechanics is used to describe molecular motion.

Gas pressure arises from momentum transfer when molecules collide elastically with the container walls. For molecules moving in the x direction, a wall collision reverses the x component of velocity while leaving the tangential components unchanged in an ideal elastic collision.

For a gas of molecules of mass m and number density n, the pressure is related to the mean square molecular speed. The isotropic distribution of random motion means the mean squares of the three velocity components are equal.
If E is the total translational kinetic energy of N molecules in volume V, pressure is two-thirds of translational kinetic energy per unit volume.
Combining the kinetic theory pressure equation with the ideal gas equation shows that average translational kinetic energy per molecule depends only on absolute temperature, not on the gas species.
The root mean square speed is the square root of the mean square molecular speed. It increases with the square root of absolute temperature and decreases with the square root of molecular mass.

At a common temperature, different ideal-gas species have the same average translational kinetic energy per molecule, but their root mean square speeds differ because their molecular masses differ. Lighter molecules have larger rms speeds.

The law of equipartition states that in thermal equilibrium, each independent quadratic term in the energy contributes an average energy of (1/2)kBT per molecule. Each translational degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kBT; each active vibrational mode has kinetic and potential terms and contributes kBT.
equations: Average energy per quadratic degree of freedom = (1/2)kBT

content.text: Degrees of freedom are independent coordinates or modes needed to describe motion or energy. A free molecule has three translational degrees of freedom. A rigid diatomic molecule has two rotational degrees of freedom about axes perpendicular to its bond, in addition to translation. Vibrational modes may contribute at suitable temperatures.
A monatomic ideal gas has three translational degrees of freedom. Its internal energy per mole is (3/2)RT, giving molar heat capacity at constant volume Cv = (3/2)R. For any ideal gas Cp − Cv = R.

metadata.topic: Specific heat capacity of a monatomic ideal gas

content.text: For a rigid diatomic ideal gas at ordinary temperatures when vibrational modes are inactive, there are three translational and two rotational degrees of freedom. The molar internal energy and heat capacities follow from equipartition.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Specific heat capacity of rigid diatomic gas

content.text: If one vibrational mode becomes active, it contributes both kinetic and potential energy. The molar internal energy and heat capacities increase compared with the rigid-diatomic model.

For a polyatomic molecule with three translational degrees of freedom, three rotational degrees of freedom and f active vibrational modes, equipartition gives the corresponding ideal-gas molar heat capacities. The number of active vibrational modes depends on the molecule and temperature.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Specific heat capacity of polyatomic gases

content.text: In the classical model, each atom in a solid vibrates about its equilibrium position. Three-dimensional vibration contributes an average energy of 3kBT per atom, predicting a molar heat capacity of approximately 3R (Dulong–Petit law). The prediction works reasonably for many solids at ordinary temperatures but has exceptions.

The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions. Molecules move rapidly but undergo frequent collisions, so their paths are repeatedly deflected. Mean free path depends inversely on number density and molecular collision cross-section.
equations: λ = 1/(nπd²) in the simplified stationary-molecule model
λ = 1/(√2 nπd²) with relative molecular motion

content.text: In the simplified model where other molecules are treated as stationary, the average time between collisions is the inverse of the collision rate. Accounting for the relative motion of molecules introduces a factor of √2 in the mean-free-path expression.

Mean free path increases as number density decreases and decreases as molecular diameter or density increases. In a highly evacuated tube, the mean free path can approach the length of the tube. Gas transport properties such as viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusion are related to molecular motion and collision behaviour.

The ideal gas equation is PV = μRT = NkBT. Real gases obey it approximately, especially at low pressure and high temperature. Boyle’s and Charles’ laws follow when the amount of gas and one other state variable are held fixed.
Kinetic theory relates pressure to mean square molecular speed and identifies absolute temperature with average translational kinetic energy. The rms speed depends on temperature and molecular mass.
Equipartition assigns (1/2)kBT to each independent quadratic energy term. The molar heat capacities depend on the active degrees of freedom, and ideal gases obey Cp − Cv = R.

content.text: Pressure exists throughout a fluid, not only at the container walls. A layer of gas in equilibrium experiences equal pressure on its two sides.

metadata.topic: Points to ponder: pressure in a fluid

content.text: At ordinary pressure and temperature, intermolecular spacing in a gas is not infinitely large compared with solids and liquids, but the mean free path is much larger than molecular size and interatomic spacing.
Each vibrational mode has kinetic and potential energy terms and therefore contributes two quadratic degrees of freedom, with total average energy kBT per molecule when the mode is active.
